intended: The mid-passage line states that timings cover the runs that reported a finish time, and that about a sixth of each depot's runs reported none. The minute figures are therefore tallied over roughly five sixths of the runs dispatched, while the claim is about delivery time on the runs the routing change was rolled out to, the non-reporting sixth included. Runs that come back without a finish time are not a random slice of the dispatch book, since late returns and rounds that were never closed out are exactly the runs most likely to have run long, so the 8, 5, 9 and 6 minute reductions recorded on the reporting subset are consistent with no reduction across all runs dispatched. The four groups run out of Kettleby Wharf, Stanmoor Yard, Devening Cross and Harkaway Point across four different months, and the same sixth goes unreported at each depot, so the spread over depots, vehicle types and months does nothing to close the gap.
reported: The timings cover a narrower population than the claim: "Timings cover the runs that reported a finish time, and about a sixth of each depot's runs reported none." Runs that never reported a finish are exactly the ones most likely to have run long, so dropping a sixth of every depot's runs can produce the 5-9 minute improvement on its own.

reported: 'Timings cover the runs that reported a finish time, and about a sixth of each depot's runs reported none' means the averages are computed on only five-sixths of the runs, excluding precisely the runs most likely to have gone wrong or run long; an 8- or 9-minute drop could come entirely from which runs fell out of the denominator.

intended: All four cohorts are starter signups from Norway via webinar inside one March window, so the trial fact stated mid-passage covers every case at once: the free trial ran thirty days, four times its length in the earlier period, and a thirty-day trial leaves users still inside their trial at week two. The scope clause beside that fact has every cohort here signed up on that trial, so the policy change reaches all four. Each cohort is compared against itself a month earlier, when the seven-day trial still applied, so the longer trial and the onboarding email moved together and the 3 to 6 point lifts cannot be attributed to the email. The population and completeness clauses in the same line leave the retention figures covering every signup, so the trial length is the whole of the defect.
reported: A competing cause reaches every cohort: "The free trial ran thirty days, four times its length in the earlier period, and every cohort here signed up on that trial." A trial extended from about a week to thirty days would by itself lift week-two retention, so the 3-6 point gains are not attributable to the onboarding email.

intended: In cases one and three the retention figure was read before the email was sent: 9 March precedes 24 March, and 10 October precedes 25 October. Half the evidence therefore describes week-two retention that was already recorded when the onboarding email went out, so it cannot be evidence for that email. Cases two and four are correctly ordered but are not enough on their own.
reported: Two cases are measured before the email went out: cohort One was 'emailed 24 March' with retention read 'by 9 March', and cohort Three was 'emailed 25 October' and read 'by 10 October' - fifteen days earlier in each case, and week-two retention would need fourteen days after the send.

intended: The mid-passage line states that rates cover the boards that reached the grading stage, and that about a tenth of each run's boards were scrapped before grading. The defect figures are therefore tallied over nine tenths of the boards built on each run, while the claim is about board defects on the run, the scrapped tenth included. Boards pulled off the line before grading are the damaged and mis-built ones, and leaving them out of the count lowers the recorded defect rate with no change at all in how many bad boards were built, so the drops of 6, 4, 7 and 5 percent are consistent with defect production holding flat. The four runs sit on the Aspen, Kestrel, Larkspur and Meridian lines across four different months, and the same tenth is scrapped before grading on each, so the spread over lines, board families and months does nothing to close the gap.
reported: The defect rate is computed on a narrower population than the claim: "Rates cover the boards that reached the grading stage, and about a tenth of each run's boards were scrapped before grading." The 10 percent scrapped pre-grading, the boards most likely to be defective, are excluded from the denominator entirely, so a fall of 4-7 percent among graded boards does not show total board defects fell.

reported: The defect rate is computed on a filtered population: "Rates cover the boards that reached the grading stage, and about a tenth of each run's boards were scrapped before grading". If the new solder profile shifts bad boards into pre-grading scrap, the 4-7 percent drop is an artifact of the missing tenth rather than fewer defects. The inspection threshold is not a confound, as it "held to the earlier period's setting exactly".

intended: All four cohorts are 40 Fenwick users on Corvid 7 phones inside one March, so the single weather fact stated mid-passage covers every case at once: outdoor temperature in each cohort's city fell ten degrees from the month before, which lowers resting heart rate on its own. The scope clause beside that fact has every cohort sleeping in unconditioned rooms open to outside air, so the cooling reaches every user whose heart rate was read. Each cohort is compared against itself in February, when the nights were warmer, rather than against an unenrolled cohort in the same month, so the cooling and the app arrived together and the 3 to 6 bpm drops cannot be attributed to the app. The population and completeness clauses in the same line leave the readings covering every enrolled user, so nothing further is wrong with the item.
reported: 'Outdoor temperature in each cohort's city fell ten degrees from the month before, and every cohort slept in unconditioned rooms open to outside air' - the ten-degree drop reached every sleeper, and cooler sleeping temperature lowers resting heart rate on its own, which fits all four cohorts and the whole 3-6 bpm effect.
